There is a kind of work the world depends on that almost no one notices, and that is precisely how you know it is being done well.

I think about this a lot — not the work of building, which gets all the monuments and the ribbon-cuttings and the TED Talks, but the work of *maintaining*. The tightening of bolts, the sweeping of floors, the patching of roofs, the restocking of shelves, the pruning of trees so they don’t take out power lines in the next storm. The people who re-paint the lines on the highway at night. The janitor who knows which radiator in the old elementary school clanks like a ghost and how to thump it just right so it goes quiet. The IT person who keeps a twenty-year-old database alive because an entire city's bus routes still run on it.

We love stories about creation. We are far less good at telling stories about preservation. A new bridge is news. A bridge that does not collapse for fifty years because someone inspected it every spring is not news, even though the second thing is arguably more impressive.

I once knew a man named Ellis who took care of a municipal swimming pool in a small town in Ohio. This was not a glamorous pool. It was built in 1968, a big outdoor rectangle with a high dive that was eventually removed for insurance reasons, and a bathhouse made of cinderblock that never quite stopped smelling faintly of chlorine even in January. Every summer, Ellis would appear in late April and start the ritual of opening it. He would test pumps older than most of the lifeguards, scrub algae off tiles, replace cracked drains, argue with the town council about the price of chemicals. For three months, thousands of kids would scream and splash and do cannonballs and learn to swim, and then over Labor Day weekend it would close and everyone would go back to school.

I asked him once if he ever got tired of doing the same thing every year. He looked at me like I’d misunderstood his job completely. He said, “It’s not the same thing every year. The water is different every year. The kids are different. The cracks are in different places.”

That has stuck with me. The idea that maintenance is not repetition, but attention. You cannot maintain something well if you are on autopilot. You have to look, every time, as if you have never seen it before, because entropy is creative. It finds new ways to undo your work. Paint peels in a new pattern. Rust blooms where it didn’t before. A kid figures out a new way to jam the locker door. The work is only boring if you aren’t paying attention.

We live in a culture that has quietly decided that maintenance is lesser work. That it’s what you do if you can’t do something more innovative or disruptive. Our economic language betrays us: we talk about “growth” as if it were the only good, and “stagnation” as if keeping things in good repair were a kind of failure. Nobody gets venture capital to keep the sidewalks even. There is no IPO for making sure the trains run on time for thirty consecutive years.

And yet, look around. Civilization is not really a collection of marvels. It is a collection of maintenance agreements. Democracy is not an election; it is the maintenance of elections — the training of poll workers, the updating of voter rolls without purging the wrong people, the boring, procedural care that makes a free election *free*. The internet is not a cloud; it is rooms full of humming servers and undersea cables and people who get paged at 3 a.m. because a router in Virginia is overheating. Your body is not a statue; it is constant maintenance — your skin replacing itself every month, your liver quietly filtering, your immune system patrolling without applause.

There is a Japanese concept I love called *kintsugi*, the art of repairing broken pottery with powdered gold, making the crack part of the history rather than hiding it. But most maintenance is not like that. Most maintenance is invisible by design. The best compliment you can give a custodian is that you never had to think about the bathroom. The best compliment for an archivist is that the documents were there when you needed them. This invisibility has a cost: we forget to value it, and we forget to fund it, until something fails catastrophically and then we act shocked.

I wonder what would happen if we taught kids to revere maintainers as much as we teach them to revere inventors. What if every science fair had a category for “kept something working beautifully for a year?” What if history classes spent as much time on the people who preserved the Library of Alexandria as on those who built it? What if we told the story of the engineer who noticed a hairline fracture in a bridge support during a routine inspection — a bridge that ten thousand people drove over every day — and reported it even though it meant paperwork and evening meetings and people being annoyed about detours?

That person saved lives in a way that never makes a plaque.

There is a humility to maintenance that I think we need right now. Building is often about ego: *Look what I made.* Maintaining is about service: *Look what I kept for you.* It requires a different relationship to time. Builders think in groundbreakings and launch dates. Maintainers think in seasons and decades. They know that very little can be fixed once and for all. Everything leaks. Everything fades. The wind will always try to take the roof again. That is not pessimism; it is just physics. The maintainer’s answer to entropy is not despair but routine. I will be here tomorrow. I will check again.

My grandmother kept a garden for fifty-two years in the same plot behind her house. It was never going to be in a magazine. It was tomatoes and cucumbers and zinnias and marigolds to keep the deer away, and a compost bin that she turned with a pitchfork long after her doctor told her she shouldn’t. People would say, “You’re still gardening?” as if there would be a point where she was *done*. She would laugh. The weeds did not retire. The soil did not finish. Gardening was not a project to complete; it was a conversation to continue.

I think that’s what maintenance really is: a conversation with the world about what matters enough to keep.

We are, at this moment in history, very good at starting things and very bad at keeping them. We start apps and abandon them. We start diets and abandon them. We start urban renewal projects and abandon them halfway through when the money runs out. We are even, in a larger sense, struggling to maintain the planet — which, it turns out, requires a lot of unglamorous, continuous care: monitoring carbon, protecting wetlands, insulating houses, repairing rather than replacing.

Perhaps the most radical thing you can do right now is to choose something and maintain it well. A friendship. A neighborhood. A bicycle. A stretch of river. A library card. To commit to the unsexy, repetitive, absolutely essential act of checking in, patching up, showing up.

There will be no parade for it. No one may ever thank you. The reward is stranger and quieter than that: one day you will realize that the thing you have been tending is still here, still good, still useful, because you stayed.

And that is its own kind of creation.

Ellis retired three years ago. The town hired a pool management company to run the pool instead. They do a fine job, I think. The chemicals are balanced. The deck gets hosed down. But last summer I went back and I noticed the old sign Ellis used to hand-paint every May — POOL RULES: NO RUNNING, NO DIVING, BE KIND — had been replaced by a printed vinyl banner. More legible, more durable, probably cheaper in the long run. Completely correct.

And I missed the hand-painted one so much it surprised me. The slightly crooked letters. The place where he’d painted over a wasp nest stain and you could still see the bump underneath if you knew where to look.

Someone had maintained that sign for twenty summers, not because it was efficient, but because it was his.
